Lena — thanks, received and reviewed. High-level answers below and attached an appendix workbook with formulas and a worked example (see Redwood_SLO_calculation_appendix.xlsx).

Summary (short):
- Primary measurement plane: Redwood uses system-observed telemetry (per-route histogram ingestion) to evaluate SLOs and trigger credits. System-observed metrics are the source of truth for contractual credits because they directly reflect the served workload inside Redwood’s runtime.
- Customer-observed telemetry (synthetic probes / SDK traces) is treated as corroborating evidence. We provide a harmonization process where probe schedules and locations are mapped to equivalent system-observed dimensions for attribution and debugging.
- Probe harmonization: we recommend a joint probe baseline (locations + cadence) that matches your production traffic footprint. For credit avoidance (false positive reduction) we apply time-window alignment and percent-drop thresholds before attributing customer-observed failures to system incidents.

Key details (please see appendix for formulas):
1) Aggregation windows: service availability is computed on rolling 30-day windows for credits; latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) are computed daily and rolled up to the monthly window using weighted histograms.
2) Attribution model: when a customer synthetic probe reports an outage, we check: (a) whether system-observed request failure rate for the same model/route exceeded the service incident threshold in the same window, and (b) whether regional capacity events or network egress anomalies were present. Only when system-observed anomalies align do we count an incident against Redwood for credits.
3) Credit formula (example): Credit = max(0, (SLO_target - Effective_availability) / SLO_target) * Monthly_fee. Effective_availability excludes scheduled maintenance windows (>15 minutes) and customer-configured traffic steering exceptions.
4) Measurement sources: time-series from Redwood console (ingested from the serving runtime), recorded trace samples, and probe logs. We retain raw telemetry for 90 days and aggregated evidence for 13 months for audit.

Next steps: happy to schedule a 30–45 minute technical walk-through. Rishi will lead the measurement deep-dive and can show the probe-harmonization playbook.

Lena — quick technical clarifications from our side before the walkthrough:

1) Probe cadence and sample size: for credit-reconciliation we ask that probes be scheduled no less frequently than once per 5 minutes from each nominated region, and at least three probe endpoints per region (to avoid single-endpoint noise). We can adopt your existing probe endpoints if you provide IPs/locations.

2) Time alignment window: we use a conservative ±3 minute alignment window when correlating probe failures with system-observed anomalies to reduce misattribution from transient network jitter. If Globex prefers a tighter window we can negotiate that in the SOW.

3) Ambiguity handling and dispute resolution: when probe vs system-observed signals disagree, we produce a reproducible evidence packet (per-incident logs, histograms, and probe traces) and engage a joint review within 5 business days. If unresolved, we escalate to an independent measurement arbiter (mutually agreed third party) as a final step — we note this in the appendix as an optional addendum.

Would you like us to pre-compute the sample 30-day rolling window using Globex’s traffic distribution (we saw you uploaded an anonymized footprint in the RFP portal)? If yes, please confirm the dataset ID.

Thanks — Rishi
